what_its_for: Tildrakizumab-asmn is used to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in adults. Plaque psoriasis is a skin condition that causes thick, red, scaly patches on your skin. This medicine works by calming down part of your immune system that causes these skin patches to form.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection under your skin (called a subcutaneous injection). It is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic or doctor's office — you do not inject this medicine yourself at home. The injection is usually given in your upper arm, thigh, or belly area. Each dose comes as a prefilled syringe that your healthcare provider will use.
dosing: The usual dose is 100 mg given as an injection under the skin. You will receive your first dose, then a second dose 4 weeks later. After that, you will receive a dose every 12 weeks (about once every 3 months). Always keep your scheduled appointments so you do not miss a dose.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled injection appointment, contact your doctor or clinic as soon as possible to reschedule. Try to get the injection as soon as you can, then continue on your regular dosing schedule from that point. Do not try to double up doses. Call your doctor if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Tildrakizumab-asmn is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. If you are ever given prefilled syringes to bring to an appointment, keep them in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze the medicine or shake it. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. If the medicine has been left out at room temperature, it should be used within 5 days. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, discolored, or contains visible particles.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as the chickenpox vaccine, MMR vaccine, or nasal flu spray) while using this medicine, as it may make those vaccines less safe or effective. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Let all of your healthcare providers know you are taking this medicine. Try to avoid close contact with people who have serious infections, as this medicine can lower your ability to fight infections.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice any of the following: signs of infection such as fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath, burning when you urinate, or a wound that will not heal; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, or dizziness; new or worsening skin rashes or sores; or if you feel generally unwell. Also tell your doctor if you have ever had tuberculosis (TB) or have been around someone with TB, and if you have HIV, hepatitis, or any other ongoing infections before starting this medicine.
when_it_works: Most people begin to see improvement in their skin within a few weeks, but it may take up to 3 to 6 months to see the full benefit of this medicine. Everyone responds differently, so be patient and continue your treatments as scheduled. Do not stop the medicine without talking to your doctor, even if your skin looks better.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): This medicine can be used in older adults, but they may have a slightly higher risk of infections. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Pregnancy: It is not known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or become pregnant while taking this medicine. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine is not currently approved for use in children or teenagers under 18 years of age. Kidney or liver problems: No dose adjustments are currently recommended, but always tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions you have.
